sessions.goal: Establish collaborative empirical framework and identify automatic thoughts related to recent professional setbacks.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Hello Elena, thank you for coming in today. Before we dive into what brought you here, I want to make sure we work together as a team to understand your experiences at your own pace. How would you like to use our time today?
turns.belief_state: Therapy is a collaborative process where the client guides the focus.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Honestly, I am not entirely sure. I just feel like everything I have built over the past ten years collapsed when I was laid off. I feel completely inadequate.
turns.belief_state: I am inherently inadequate compared to my peers.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That sounds like a heavy burden to carry, especially when your career has been such a big part of your life. When you use the word inadequate, what specific thoughts or images go through your mind?
turns.belief_state: Exploring specific thoughts helps clarify the cognitive triad.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I picture myself sitting in interviews, completely exposed as a fraud who only got her past jobs by accident. I think, 'Every mistake I make proves I do not belong in this field.'
turns.belief_state: Every mistake I make proves I do not belong in this field.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That is a very painful prediction to hold about yourself. Notice how that thought treats a single layoff as absolute proof of your entire capability. Would you be willing to treat that thought as a working hypothesis we can test together, rather than an absolute fact?
turns.belief_state: Automatic thoughts can be examined objectively as hypotheses.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I suppose we could look at it, but it feels pretty real. It feels like basic common sense given my current situation.
turns.belief_state: My negative feelings validate my negative beliefs.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: It makes total sense that it feels that way when emotion and thought are so intertwined. Between now and our next session, would you be open to noticing moments when this thought pops up and briefly writing down what was happening right before?
turns.belief_state: Behavioral self-monitoring builds awareness of cognitive triggers.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Yes, I can try to log them. I might forget or feel silly doing it, but I can try.
turns.belief_state: I will try the homework even though I feel doubtful.

sessions.ending_state: Established initial collaborative stance; client agreed to track automatic thoughts despite some lingering skepticism.

sessions.goal: Examine thought logs, address a minor therapeutic rupture regarding perceived pressure, and refine the cognitive conceptualization.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Welcome back, Elena. How did the week go with tracking your thoughts? Remember, whatever happened—or didn't happen—is valuable information for us.
turns.belief_state: Client safety and comfort take precedence over completed homework.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I did it for three days and then I stopped. Looking at the list made me feel even more broken. It felt like you gave me homework just to prove how dysfunctional I am.
turns.belief_state: The therapist is judging me and pushing me too hard.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: I am really glad you told me that. I apologize if my suggestion felt like an assignment to grade your dysfunction. That is the exact opposite of what I intended. Can we look at what happened right before you felt that way?
turns.belief_state: Ruptures must be addressed immediately to maintain collaboration.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I just felt like if I did not fill out the log perfectly, I was failing therapy too. Like I cannot even be a good client.
turns.belief_state: If I am not constantly productive, I have no value.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Ah, look at that core rule appearing right here in our room: 'If I am not constantly productive or doing it right, I have no value.' Even in therapy, your mind is applying that pressure.
turns.belief_state: Core beliefs manifest in the immediate therapeutic relationship.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Oh. Wow. I did not even see that happening until you pointed it out. I was doing it to myself.
turns.belief_state: My automatic self-criticism applies to everything I do.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: You are not alone in it; our minds love to automate these rules. Knowing this now, how should we adjust our approach so it feels helpful rather than like a test?
turns.belief_state: The client must help design their own experiments.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Maybe we focus less on logs and more on talking through specific recent moments without pressure to get it right.
turns.belief_state: I have a say in how therapy is conducted.

sessions.ending_state: Successfully navigated a minor therapeutic rupture, uncovering a core belief about productivity operating within the session itself.

sessions.goal: Design and review a behavioral experiment to test the prediction that making a mistake leads to total rejection.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Hello Elena. How are you feeling today following our conversation last week about the pressure to be a 'good client'?
turns.belief_state: Checking in on relational repair promotes safety.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I have been feeling a bit lighter. I realized I do not have to ace therapy. But I still feel terrified of reaching out to old professional contacts because I am afraid they will judge my layoff.
turns.belief_state: Reaching out will confirm my inadequacy.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That fear makes complete sense given how much weight you place on professional standing. Would you be up for designing a small behavioral experiment to test what actually happens when you reach out to someone low-stakes?
turns.belief_state: Behavioral experiments are superior to verbal dispute alone.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: What kind of experiment? Like emailing a former colleague I barely knew?
turns.belief_state: Experiments might be uncomfortable.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That could work. We could define what you predict they will think, and then see what they actually reply. What is your strongest prediction?
turns.belief_state: Identifying explicit predictions allows for empirical testing.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: My prediction is they will ignore my email or think I am desperately looking for a handout.
turns.belief_state: Others view me with contempt.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Let us test that hypothesis. If you sent a brief, casual check-in note this week, what would be the worst-case scenario, and how would you cope with it?
turns.belief_state: Coping planning reduces anxiety about potential negative outcomes.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: The worst case is silence, which would hurt, but I suppose I survived worse this month. Okay, I will try sending one message to Sarah by Thursday.
turns.belief_state: I can tolerate difficult outcomes to test my assumptions.

sessions.ending_state: Collaboratively designed a behavioral experiment focused on reaching out to a former colleague, establishing coping strategies for worst-case outcomes.

sessions.goal: 建立咨询同盟，识别林伟在跨部门会议中的自动思维与灾难化预测。

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 林伟你好，欢迎来到咨询室。我们今天可以从近期让你觉得最有挑战的一个场景开始谈起。
turns.belief_state: 咨询师需要通过开放式提问了解当事人的主诉

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 谢谢。其实上周公司开跨部门例会的时候，我准备了一个汇报。当我说到一半看到设计总监皱了一下眉头，我脑子里马上就炸了，觉得我讲得简直一塌糊涂，他们肯定觉得我这个主管名不副实。
turns.belief_state: 如果我在开会时说错一句话，大家就会彻底否定我的能力

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 听到设计总监皱眉，你立刻联想到自己的能力会被全盘否定，这让你感到了强烈的焦虑。我们来看看，当时在你脑海里闪过的那个最坏的想法具体是什么？
turns.belief_state: 需要引导当事人捕捉具体的自动思维

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 我的想法就是‘我完蛋了，我根本不配做这个主管，所有人都在心里嘲笑我’。而且我觉得我必须表现得完美，一旦有一点瑕疵，就全盘皆输。
turns.belief_state: 我必须表现得完美无瑕，否则就不配拥有目前的职位

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 这是一个非常典型的‘非黑即白’和‘灾难化’的思维过程。你看，设计总监皱眉，可能有很多种原因，比如他当时想到了别的工作难题。但你直接把它画等号成了对你的否定。你觉得这种思维方式对你产生了什么影响？
turns.belief_state: 通过合作性审视帮助当事人将客观事实与主观解释剥离

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 影响就是我接下来讲的内容开始结巴，甚至恨不得找个地缝钻进去，后面根本无法专心开会了。但我总觉得我的直觉是对的，别人就是讨厌我。
turns.belief_state: 当事人的自动化认知根深蒂固，对替代解释产生怀疑

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 我完全理解这种强烈的直觉体验，它保护你不去面对可能的伤害。不过，既然这只是一个假设，我们能不能在接下来的两周里，把它当作一个待检验的‘实验’，而不是绝对的真理？
turns.belief_state: 确立基于认知行为框架的实验导向

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 当作实验？我不知道我有没有勇气去验证，但我愿意尝试看看，虽然我还是觉得很没底。
turns.belief_state: 当事人表现出有限的开放性，但仍伴随不安全感

sessions.ending_state: 建立了初步的认知行为契约，识别了核心的灾难化信念，当事人在犹豫中同意尝试行为实验。

sessions.goal: 回顾上一周的行为实验，处理由于实验结果不明确导致的理解偏差和咨询关系中的小摩擦。

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 林伟，过去这一周过得怎么样？我们之前商量的小实验，你在周三的部门会议上有尝试去观察大家的真实反应吗？
turns.belief_state: 评估上周布置的家庭作业执行情况

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 我试了。我在会上发言时特意看了看大家的脸，结果产品经理一直看着手机，运营主管好像叹了口气。我觉得我的实验失败了，他们根本不在乎我，甚至觉得我很烦。
turns.belief_state: 别人脸上的冷淡表情意味着他们正在厌恶我

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 听到你这么说，我能感觉到你此刻的失望。不过，运营主管叹气和产品经理看手机，直接就能证明他们觉得你很烦、在厌恶你吗？我们能不能把这些细节再仔细拆解一下？
turns.belief_state: 指出当事人的情感推理谬误

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: （声音变大）你为什么总觉得我在小题大做？每次我都觉得很痛苦，但你好像总是在挑我逻辑上的毛病，这让我觉得你根本没有真正体会到我在职场上的压力！
turns.belief_state: 咨询关系出现轻微裂痕，当事人感到被辩驳而非被理解

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 谢谢你这么直接地告诉我你的感受。我刚才的语气可能显得太急于纠正你的想法了，让你觉得我在否定你的痛苦，这并不是我的本意。我向你道歉。你的痛苦和焦虑是百分之百真实的。
turns.belief_state: 及时修复咨询关系裂痕，优先确认当事人的情绪体验

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 听到你这么说……我好受了一些。我只是太害怕自己是个失败者了，所以听到你分析时，我第一反应觉得你也在嫌弃我表现得不好。
turns.belief_state: 当事人展露更深层的防御心理和对评价的恐惧

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 原来你把我的理性探讨，不自觉地翻译成了‘批评’，这就像你在开会时把同事的无意识举动翻译成‘厌恶’一样。这是一个非常宝贵的觉察。你觉得呢？
turns.belief_state: 将咨询室内的互动与外部社交情境建立类比

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 好像真的是这样……我总是带着一副‘随时准备挨批评’的有色眼镜在看周围的一切。看来我不仅对同事这样，对你也是这样。
turns.belief_state: 当事人成功将内部体验泛化并获得新认知

sessions.ending_state: 成功处理了咨询过程中的关系裂痕，深化了对‘有色眼镜’自动思维的理解，但焦虑情绪并未完全根除。

sessions.goal: 整合前两周的觉察，设计更具针对性的微型行为实验，探索完美主义背后的规则。

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 林伟，经过上周的讨论，这周你带着‘随时准备挨批评的有色眼镜’这个视角，去看待工作和生活，有什么新的发现吗？
turns.belief_state: 鼓励当事人自主回顾生活中的认知重构应用

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 这周确实有改变。周四有个跨部门的非正式午餐，我本来想借口加班不去的，但我想起了咱们的讨论，就硬着头皮去了。结果发现大家其实在聊周末的电影，根本没人盯着我的表现。
turns.belief_state: 通过行为实验获取了反证灾难化预测的新证据

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 太棒了！你不仅去了，而且还留心观察到了真实的社交场景并不是你想象的‘批斗大会’。这带给你什么感受？
turns.belief_state: 强化当事人的正向积极体验

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 虽然去了，但我在那坐着的时候手心还是出汗，心里一直紧绷着，总觉得‘我只是这次运气好没被点名，下次肯定会露馅’。
turns.belief_state: 旧有的核心信念仍在发挥作用，表现为折扣正向事件

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 即使有了好结果，大脑还是会加上一个‘不过运气好’的限定词。这背后是不是有一个更深的信念在支撑？比如：‘我必须永远不出错，才能证明我的安全’？
turns.belief_state: 引导当事人触及更深层的规则或图式

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 对，我从小到大家里对我的要求就是这样，考98分都会被问为什么不是100分。所以我潜意识里觉得，只要我犯一次错，我的人生就会崩塌。
turns.belief_state: 家庭背景对当事人 perfectionism 的影响浮出水面

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 带着这样的成长背景走到今天，你一路真的很不容易。过去的规则保护了你取得成就，但也让你在社交中精疲力竭。接下来，我们可以一起思考，如何为这个‘必须完美’的规则制定一个更有弹性的替代版本。
turns.belief_state: 协助当事人构建替代性中间信念

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 也许我可以试着告诉自己：‘犯错是学习的一部分，即使表现不完美，我依然是一个有价值的专业人员。’听起来有点陌生，但我愿意让它成为我新的座右铭。
turns.belief_state: 当事人自主生成了更具适应性的信念体系

sessions.ending_state: 当事人成功完成了行为实验，触及了完美的童年渊源，并自发生成了更具弹性的应对信念，咨询进入巩固阶段。

sessions.goal: Introduce the collaborative cognitive model and examine Elena's catastrophic interpretations of somatic arousal.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Hello Elena, thank you for coming in today. As we begin, I'd love to hear a bit about what brings you here and what you're hoping we might explore together.
turns.belief_state: Collaborative exploration is essential to understanding the client's perspective.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Hi. Honestly, I've been feeling completely overwhelmed lately. Over the past couple of months, out of nowhere, my heart will start racing while I'm at my desk, and my immediate thought is that something terrible is happening to my body.
turns.belief_state: Any sudden change in my physical state means a catastrophic medical emergency is beginning.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That sounds deeply distressing to experience while simply sitting at your desk. When that sudden racing heart happens, what goes through your mind about what it might mean?
turns.belief_state: Identifying automatic thoughts helps map the connection between bodily cues and fear.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I immediately think I'm having a cardiac event or losing control entirely. And once that thought hits, I feel like I have to stop everything and monitor every single beat.
turns.belief_state: If I cannot immediately control my heartbeat, I will completely lose control of my life.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: It makes complete sense that you would try to monitor and protect yourself when your mind interprets the sensation that way. In CBT, we often look at how our thoughts, physical sensations, and behaviors form a loop. Would it be alright if we map out what happened during one of these recent episodes together?
turns.belief_state: Co-creating a formulation empowers the client to see patterns without judgment.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I guess so. But sometimes it feels like these physical sensations are just too real to be 'just thoughts.' What if we miss something physical?
turns.belief_state: Physical sensations are definitive proof of danger until proven otherwise.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That is a very valid concern, and it's completely understandable to want to rule out physical causes. We aren't dismissing your bodily sensations at all; rather, we want to look at all the pieces of the puzzle—including how our interpretation of a sensation can actually amplify the physical response itself.
turns.belief_state: Validating safety concerns while introducing the cognitive model reduces resistance.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: When you put it that way, I can see how watching my heart rate so closely might actually make it beat faster. It just feels like a very hard habit to break.
turns.belief_state: Perhaps these physical sensations are simply anxiety responses, though it feels too risky to assume that.

sessions.ending_state: Initial formulation established with minor skepticism regarding the purely cognitive nature of somatic symptoms.

sessions.goal: Review thought logs and design a behavioral experiment to test the hypothesis about somatic monitoring.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Hello Elena. How has your week been, and how did you find tracking those physical sensations and automatic thoughts since our last meeting?
turns.belief_state: Reviewing self-monitoring data bridges session insights into daily practice.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: It was mixed. I tried writing them down, but honestly, during a couple of moments at work when my chest felt tight, I completely forgot to use the log. I just went straight back to checking my pulse.
turns.belief_state: If I can't execute the technique perfectly, I am failing at therapy.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: First, let's normalize that completely. When anxiety spikes, our prefrontal cortex goes offline a bit—our brain's alarm system takes over. The fact that you noticed the urge to check your pulse is actually a huge step of awareness.
turns.belief_state: Reframing setbacks as awareness opportunities prevents self-criticism.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I suppose so. But I still feel stuck believing that if I don't check my heart rate, something catastrophic will happen unchecked.
turns.belief_state: Monitoring is the only thing standing between me and disaster.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That core belief is working overtime. Would you be open to running a small, safe behavioral experiment this week to test what actually happens when we intentionally drop the safety behavior of pulse-checking for just two minutes?
turns.belief_state: Behavioral experiments provide experiential data that challenges rigid beliefs.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Just two minutes without checking? That sounds terrifying. What if my heart doesn't slow down?
turns.belief_state: Dropping safety behaviors will lead to unmanageable escalation.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: We would design it together when you feel ready, and we can even practice a mild version right here in the room where you are completely safe. What do you think about testing that hypothesis together?
turns.belief_state: Collaborative pacing ensures the client retains agency over exposure tasks.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Okay. Doing it here with you feels a bit more manageable than doing it alone at work. Let's try it.
turns.belief_state: I can test my beliefs in a controlled, supportive environment.

sessions.ending_state: Agreement reached to conduct an in-session behavioral experiment regarding somatic monitoring.

sessions.goal: Evaluate the outcome of the behavioral experiment and address emerging friction around emotional control.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Welcome back, Elena. Last time we talked about trying an in-session test of dropping your pulse-checking. How did that feel when we did it, and did you attempt anything similar during the week?
turns.belief_state: Processing behavioral experiment outcomes consolidates new learning.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Well, in the office here, I survived it. But during the week, I tried it while working on a tight design deadline, and it didn't work. My anxiety just got louder, and I ended up checking anyway. I feel like I ruined the progress.
turns.belief_state: A single relapse means the therapeutic approach is ineffective for me.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: I hear how discouraging that felt in the heat of the moment. But I notice you're using words like 'ruined' and 'didn't work.' Let's look at the data: when you checked your pulse after feeling that spike, what did you learn?
turns.belief_state: Examining setbacks as data points prevents all-or-nothing thinking.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I learned that I'm still terrified of my own body. It feels like you're telling me to just ignore danger, and my family background taught me that ignoring warning signs leads to failure.
turns.belief_state: Rupture moment: feeling misunderstood or pushed too fast.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: I'm really glad you said that, Elena. I appreciate you letting me know that it felt like I was asking you to ignore real danger or dismiss your upbringing. That wasn't my intention at all. Can we pause and look at how that family value of high vigilance might be showing up here?
turns.belief_state: Acknowledge and repair therapeutic ruptures immediately by honoring the client's perspective.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Yeah... my parents always worked twice as hard and watched out for every obstacle. In our house, letting your guard down meant you weren't trying hard enough.
turns.belief_state: Vigilance is tied to deep-seated family values of survival and success.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That makes so much sense. Vigilance kept your family safe and successful. No wonder your body treats a racing heart as an emergency—it’s trying to be maximally alert. How can we honor that protective instinct without letting it run your life?
turns.belief_state: Reframing hyperarousal as a protective mechanism bridges cultural context with CBT.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I never thought of it as my body trying to protect me. I always thought it was betraying me. Maybe... maybe we can look at thanking it instead of fighting it?
turns.belief_state: My body's signals are protective responses rather than catastrophic failures.

sessions.ending_state: Successful repair of rupture; shift from adversarial view of bodily sensations to a compassionate, protective framework.

sessions.goal: 建立咨询同盟，收集当前的财务焦虑背景，并识别出主要的自动思维。

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 林晓你好，欢迎来到今天的咨询。我们可以先花一点时间聊聊最近让你感到最困扰的事情。
turns.belief_state: 咨询师需要倾听并建立安全信任的环境。

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 谢谢。最近其实挺糟糕的，几笔尾款被退回后，我整天都在失眠，觉得全盘皆输。
turns.belief_state: 我无法应对目前的财务危机。

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 听到尾款退回给你带来了这么大的压力，这种财务和心理上的双重冲击确实非常不好受。你刚才提到‘全盘皆输’，当我们这么想的时候，心里会有怎样的感受呢？
turns.belief_state: 自动思维与情绪之间存在紧密联系，需要温和地引导察觉。

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 就觉得我这几年完全是白干了。我连最基础的财务都搞不定，我怎么配做一个独立的自由职业者？
turns.belief_state: 我什么都做不好，连最基础的财务管理都处理不好。

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 这是一个很沉重的结论。‘我连最基础的财务都搞不定’，这句话背后好像包含着对自己全盘的否定。如果我们把这个想法当成一个有待检验的假设，而不是绝对的事实，你觉得可以吗？
turns.belief_state: 通过协作性经验主义可以开始松动绝对化的认知。

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 可是事实就是这样啊，银行退回支票就是因为我的结算流程出了问题，这就是我的错。
turns.belief_state: 外部事件直接等于个人完全失败。

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 我完全理解你此刻的自责。结算流程遇到了困难，这属于客观事实；但‘这就是我的错、我整个人都失败了’，这两者之间似乎画了一个等号。这也是我们后续可以一起仔细看看的地方。
turns.belief_state: 需要厘清客观事件与全盘自我否定的界限。

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 听你这么说，我心里稍微松了一口气，但还是觉得很恐慌，不知道明天交房租怎么办。
turns.belief_state: 现实困难依然存在，焦虑并未完全消除。

sessions.ending_state: 初步建立了信任同盟，识别出了核心的自动思维，但客户对客观事件与自身价值的混淆仍较严重。

sessions.goal: 审查上周记录的自动思维日记，并对‘如果工作失误就代表彻底失败’的认知进行苏格拉底式提问。

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 林晓，这周过得怎么样？上周我们布置的自动思维日记，你尝试记录了吗？
turns.belief_state: 家庭作业可以帮助客户在日常生活中应用CBT工具。

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 记录了几天，但我发现越记录越烦躁。每次写下那些想法，我都觉得自己特别无能，甚至有点不想来做今天的咨询了。
turns.belief_state: 记录负面想法会引发防御和逃避。

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 谢谢你这么坦诚地告诉我你的抗拒。这其实非常重要，当我们在面对痛苦的想法时，本能就会想逃避。你刚才提到写完觉得自己很无能，这是不是意味着写日记本身变成了另一种惩罚你的工具？
turns.belief_state: 觉察并处理治疗过程中的阻抗与小挫折。

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 对……我就是在拿这些证据证明自己多么糟糕。你看，连咨询作业我都做得让你不满意吧？
turns.belief_state: 把咨询关系也纳入了自我批评的框架中。

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 在这里没有‘满意或不满意’的考试，林晓。你的任何反应都是被允许的。让我们看看你写下的其中一条：‘如果我的工作出现失误，说明我整个人都是失败的。’我们能一起来检验一下这个绝对化的说法吗？
turns.belief_state: 转移焦点回到核心信念的检验上。

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 如果按这个逻辑，我以前成功交付过那么多设计项目，它们算什么？但我的脑子里好像总有一个声音在抹杀过去的成绩。
turns.belief_state: 开始注意到认知偏误（选择性过滤）。

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 这个‘脑子里的声音’抓得很紧。如果我们列一张清单，一边是这次退票的客观事实，另一边是过去三年的专业成果，它们能同时存在吗？
turns.belief_state: 通过证据检验打破全或无的思维模式。

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 能同时存在……虽然理智上知道，但情感上还是觉得眼前的困难像座大山压着。
turns.belief_state: 认知开始松动，但情感习惯需要更多时间转化。

sessions.ending_state: 处理了客户对记录日记的抗拒与误解，客户开始在理性层面松动绝对化思维，但情绪层面的无力感依然存在。

sessions.goal: 设计行为实验，检验‘当前经济环境与结算流程存在客观困难’这一替代性信念，并评估实验结果。

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 林晓，这周我们来做一个具体的行为实验。你愿意尝试主动联系银行和那家公司的财务部门，去核对退票的具体行政原因吗？
turns.belief_state: 通过小型行为实验获取新证据以修正旧信念。

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 老实说，我非常抗拒打电话，我怕听到别人冷冰冰地拒绝或者指责我。
turns.belief_state: 预期对方会带来严厉的指责。

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 这种恐惧完全可以理解。如果我们把这次打电话看成是一次‘科学实验’，而不是去接受审判，结果无论如何，我们都只是在收集数据，你觉得呢？
turns.belief_state: 重新定义行为的性质可以降低焦虑水平。

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 好吧，我也想知道到底卡在哪个环节。如果不是我的设计问题，而是他们系统升级呢？我愿意试一试。
turns.belief_state: 客户展现出行动意愿和agency。

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 太棒了，看到你愿意迈出这一步。实验做完后，你发现真实情况是什么样的？
turns.belief_state: 回顾行为实验的实际发生情况。

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 打完电话我惊呆了，对方财务说因为银行新系统对接，他们有一半的自由职业者尾款都被退回了，根本不是针对我个人！
turns.belief_state: 外部客观事实推翻了‘我整个人失败’的假设。

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 这是一个非常有力的数据。当事实摆在眼前时，你对‘我什么都做不好’这个想法有了什么新的看法？
turns.belief_state: 巩固行为实验带来的认知转变。

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 我觉得我以前太快把所有责任揽到自己身上了。虽然钱还没到账，但至少我不用再盲目地苛责自己了。
turns.belief_state: 或许我的专业能力并非一无是处，只是当前的经济环境和结算流程确实存在客观困难。

sessions.ending_state: 通过行为实验成功检验了替代性信念，客户显著减轻了自我归因的羞耻感，能够客观看待外部环境的影响。

sessions.goal: Establish rapport, clarify the presenting problem, and introduce the cognitive model using the collaborative formulation.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Hello Elena. Welcome to our first session. I want to thank you for coming in today. How would you like to use our time?
turns.belief_state: Therapy is a collaborative journey.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Hi. Thanks for having me. Honestly, I feel a bit nervous because I am not sure I can explain my problems clearly. I just feel like I am failing at my job most of the time.
turns.belief_state: I might not be articulate enough or capable of doing this right.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: It is completely normal to feel nervous at the start. You do not need to have it all figured out. When you say you feel like you are failing, what kinds of thoughts or situations bring that up?
turns.belief_state: The client needs gentle pacing and validation.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Whenever my art director gives feedback, even if it is just a minor revision, my mind immediately jumps to 'They realize you are a fraud.' I spend hours overworking just to hide the fact that I don't know what I am doing.
turns.belief_state: I am fundamentally incompetent and must hide my flaws.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That sounds exhausting. If we look at how your thoughts, physical feelings, and behaviors connect—what we call the cognitive model—how does working extra hours affect your anxiety in the long run?
turns.belief_state: Connecting thoughts and behaviors will help illuminate the maintenance cycle.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Well, it keeps me safe temporarily, but I guess it just exhausts me more and makes me believe that the only reason I succeeded was because I spent twice as much time on it.
turns.belief_state: My successes are just the result of overcompensation, not skill.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That is a really powerful observation, Elena. You are attributing your success to the extra time rather than your actual talent. Would you be open to exploring this belief together over the next few weeks?
turns.belief_state: Collaborative goal setting will foster agency.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Yes, I would like that. I am tired of living in fear of being found out.
turns.belief_state: Maybe change is possible, though it feels scary.

sessions.ending_state: Rapport established; initial cognitive model introduced with shared understanding of overcompensation.

sessions.goal: Examine the evidence for the core belief 'I am fundamentally incompetent' and identify cognitive distortions.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Hi Elena, how has your week been since we last spoke? Did anything particular come up regarding that rule about overcompensating?
turns.belief_state: Checking in on homework and bridging sessions.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: It was tough. On Wednesday, my manager praised my branding proposal, but instead of feeling good, I immediately thought she was just being nice because she felt sorry for me.
turns.emotional_state: Frustrated and dismissive of positive feedback
turns.belief_state: Positive feedback is invalid or pity-driven.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Ah, let's look at that. Your mind discounted the positive feedback. What evidence do you have that she was only being nice versus genuine appreciation?
turns.belief_state: Examining evidence helps challenge discounting the positive.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I don't know... she specifically mentioned the color palette and the layout alignment. But anyone could have put those together. It didn't take any special genius.
turns.belief_state: If it is easy for me, it has no value.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Wait, let's pause there. Sometimes when we are close to our own work, we minimize our contribution. Does 'anyone' really design that way, or is that your internal critic speaking?
turns.belief_state: Distinguishing between objective reality and the inner critic.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I suppose not everyone. My coworker struggled with a similar layout last month. But still, that doesn't mean I am competent overall.
turns.belief_state: One instance doesn't disprove the overarching core belief of incompetence.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That is a fair point—one success doesn't instantly rewrite a lifelong belief. But it is a data point against the idea that you are entirely incompetent. How does it feel to look at it as a mixed picture?
turns.belief_state: Nuance is necessary when dismantling rigid core beliefs.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: It feels uncomfortable. It is easier to just believe I am bad at everything than to accept I am sometimes good and sometimes make mistakes.
turns.belief_state: Uncertainty is harder to manage than familiar negative self-labels.

sessions.ending_state: Identified discounting of positive feedback; client experienced mild discomfort with nuance.

sessions.goal: Design and review a behavioral experiment to test the belief about making a single mistake.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Elena, last week we talked about how black-and-white thinking keeps the fear of mistakes alive. Today, I am wondering if we can design a small experiment to test what actually happens when a minor imperfection occurs.
turns.belief_state: Behavioral experiments are essential for belief modification.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: What kind of experiment? Are you asking me to submit intentionally bad work? Because I cannot do that; my job is on the line.
turns.belief_state: Therapist wants me to sabotage my career.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Oh, not at all! I am so glad you spoke up because I clearly didn't explain myself well. I would never ask you to jeopardize your work. I meant leaving a minor, non-critical detail unpolished—like skipping an extra round of kerning on an internal draft.
turns.belief_state: Address the rupture/misunderstanding immediately.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Oh. Okay. I misunderstood. Even so, just leaving kerning undone sounds terrifying. What if someone notices and thinks I am lazy?
turns.belief_state: Imperfection equals being perceived as lazy or incompetent.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That fear makes total sense given your background. Let's write down that prediction: 'If I leave minor kerning unchecked, someone will think I am lazy and incompetent.' What is the worst that could happen, realistically?
turns.belief_state: Testing catastrophic predictions through structured questioning.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: They might ask me to fix it. Which is basically what happens anyway when I overwork, except I wouldn't have spent two extra hours doing it.
turns.belief_state: The consequence of a mistake is manageable.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Precisely. So the experiment would be to test this hypothesis this week on one low-stakes internal draft. Are you willing to try that, or does it still feel too risky?
turns.belief_state: Client must consent to the experiment's parameters.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: It still feels risky, but... I am willing to try it on the team mood board draft. That feels safe enough.
turns.belief_state: I can take a manageable risk.

sessions.ending_state: Resolved misunderstanding about experiments; agreed on a safe behavioral test for the upcoming week.

sessions.goal: Review the behavioral experiment, address residual avoidance, and consolidate gains.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Welcome back, Elena. How did the mood board experiment go? Did you manage to leave that draft unpolished?
turns.belief_state: Reviewing experimental data reinforces new learning.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I did it, but I won't lie, my stomach was in knots all morning. I submitted it and closed my laptop immediately so I wouldn't stare at it.
turns.belief_state: Doing the experiment caused anxiety, but I survived.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That took a lot of courage. What actually happened after you submitted it?
turns.belief_state: Focusing on actual outcomes rather than predicted catastrophes.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Nothing happened! Nobody mentioned the kerning. My supervisor just said 'Looks great, let's go with this direction.' I was shocked.
turns.belief_state: My catastrophic predictions did not come true.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That is fascinating data. What does that tell you about your prediction that a single imperfection leads to disaster?
turns.belief_state: Integrating the counter-evidence into cognitive schemas.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: It tells me I might be holding myself to an impossible standard that nobody else even cares about. But I still feel like next time might be different—like I just got lucky.
turns.belief_state: Old core beliefs die hard; 'luck' dismissal persists.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: It is completely natural for the old belief to try and protect you by calling it 'luck.' We don't have to erase all doubt today. How can we take what you learned and apply it moving forward?
turns.belief_state: Change is gradual; acknowledging ongoing vulnerability.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I think I can try one more experiment next week, maybe with a client-facing draft. But I will want to talk through it with you first.
turns.belief_state: Client is taking active ownership of her therapeutic progress.

sessions.ending_state: Successful experiment review with acknowledged residual self-doubt and plans for continued graded exposure.

sessions.goal: 建立咨询同盟并初步探索晓晴近期的主要困扰与自动思维

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 晓晴，你好。欢迎来到咨询室。最近这段时间，我看到你在预约表里提到了一些学业和情绪上的压力，能跟我说说你最近最想聊聊的是什么吗？
turns.belief_state: 来访者拥有自主探索自身困扰的能力

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 老师好。其实我挺不知道从哪里开始的。就是觉得每天都很累，什么都不想做，上大学这几个月好像把以前积攒的自信全用光了。
turns.belief_state: 我是一个彻底的失败者，连简单的大学生活都应付不好。

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 听到你用“把自信全用光了”来形容，这半年对你来说一定非常不易。能具体说说是哪些事情让你有了这种感觉吗？
turns.belief_state: 理解来访者的主观体验是后续合作的基础

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 期末考试成绩出来后，我的微积分只考了及格线边缘。我从小到大数学都没这么差过。还有上周社团活动，大家都在聊天，我一句话也插不上，觉得自己特别多余。
turns.belief_state: 我必须在各方面都表现完美，否则我的努力毫无价值。

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 一次微积分成绩的滑坡，加上社团里短暂的插不上话，在你的脑海里是不是迅速引发了一些更深的想法？比如，这些事情对你来说意味着什么？
turns.belief_state: 帮助来访者连接具体事件与自动思维

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 就是觉得……我根本不适合这里。我考上大学可能只是运气好，其实我就是个笨蛋，连维持正常生活都做不到。
turns.belief_state: 如果别人看到真实的我有多糟糕，他们一定会离开我。

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 你看，刚才我们聊到这里的时候，你提到了“运气好”和“觉得自己是个笨蛋”。在CBT里，我们把这种瞬间闪过的、倾向于苛刻否定自己的想法叫做自动思维。今天我们不急着去改变它，只是试着把它像照片一样抓拍下来，你觉得呢？
turns.belief_state: 认知行为治疗需要将思维外化并共同检视

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 抓拍下来……好像确实每次考试考砸或者一个人在宿舍待着时，脑子里就会自动跳出这些话，让我更不想出门了。
turns.belief_state: 开始察觉到自动思维对情绪和行为的影响

sessions.ending_state: 建立了初步合作关系，识别并记录了核心的自动思维，来访者情绪略有缓解但仍显沉重

sessions.goal: 审视自动思维的证据，引入行为激活的初步概念

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 晓晴，过去这一周过得怎么样？上周我们尝试记录了几个自动思维，你有什么新的发现吗？
turns.belief_state: 复盘有助于巩固上周的认知觉察

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 我记了几天，但我发现我根本找不到反驳它们的证据。比如我觉得自己“连简单生活都应付不好”，我看室友们既能搞定学习又能到处玩，我确实就是做不到。
turns.belief_state: 我的自我否定都是客观事实，没有反驳空间。

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 你刚才说“我看室友们既能搞定学习又能到处玩”，这里好像有一个比较的标准。我们能不能像科学家做实验一样，看看“应付不好”这个绝对的词，在现实中是不是100%成立的？
turns.belief_state: 通过苏格拉底式提问引导来访者检验绝对化思维

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 可是微积分确实及格边缘啊，这也是事实。老师，你是不是觉得我太矫情了，别人都能适应，为什么我就不行？
turns.belief_state: 别人都能适应，只有我不行，咨询师可能也在责备我。

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 晓晴，我听到你觉得我可能在认为你“矫情”，甚至让你感到有些被误解或者指责了。非常感谢你能直接把这个感受说出来。我绝对没有觉得你矫情，我只是看到你背负了太重的完美主义包袱。你愿意我们一起看看刚才那句话是怎么让你感到难受的吗？
turns.belief_state: 及时处理咨询中的人际微型断裂至关重要

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 听到你这么说……我才稍微放松一点。我太害怕别人用这种眼光看我了，因为我自己就是这么狠狠责备自己的。
turns.belief_state: 自我苛求是导致焦虑和回避的核心动力

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 是的，我们常常用最严苛的标准审判自己。既然这周我们在学习识别思维，那要不要试着做一个小小的行为实验？比如，在宿舍里不再完全孤立自己，尝试和室友进行一次十五分钟的非学业对话，看看“别人会离开我”的预测会不会发生？
turns.belief_state: 行为实验是打破认知僵局的有效手段

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 十五分钟……听起来有点冒险，但我可以试试看，大不了也就是像现在这样呗。
turns.belief_state: 来访者展现出初步的行动意愿和心理弹性

sessions.ending_state: 成功修复了中途产生的小型情绪断裂，来访者同意进行第一次行为实验，但对结果仍存顾虑

sessions.goal: 评估行为实验结果，探索底层的核心信念

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 晓晴，上周我们约定的行为实验后来进展得怎么样？那次和室友的聊天还顺利吗？
turns.belief_state: 评估实验结果是CBT疗效的关键步骤

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 其实……比我想象的好一点。我那天鼓起勇气跟室友吐槽了一下食堂的饭菜，结果她顺着聊了好久，还带我一起去买了一杯奶茶。并没有出现我想象中那种“觉得我很无聊然后离开”的场面。
turns.belief_state: 现实经验与灾难化预测存在不一致

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 太棒了！听到你愿意主动迈出这一步，我为你感到高兴。当我们把“别人一定会离开我”这个绝对预测放到现实里去检验时，你发现了什么不同？
turns.belief_state: 强化积极的认知重构经验

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 说明可能……我并没有我想象的那么讨人厌吧。但我心里还是有个声音说，这只是一次意外，下次她们就会发现我其实很无趣。
turns.belief_state: 根深蒂固的核心信念不会因一次实验轻易改变

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 这个声音很顽固，它一直在保护你，但也让你很辛苦。你看，这个声音背后是不是藏着一个更深层的信念：‘我必须完美、必须时刻有趣，否则我不配被爱’？
turns.belief_state: 引导来访者从自动思维触及中间信念与核心信念

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 对……我从小就是这样。我爸妈对我要求很高，我只有考第一名或者表现得很乖，他们才会露出笑容。如果我搞砸了，我就觉得自已毫无价值。
turns.belief_state: 核心信念根植于早期的家庭互动模式

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 谢谢你分享这段经历，这让我们看到了这个信念的来源。它在过去保护你获得了认可，但在现在的大学里，它是不是变成了一副沉重的盔甲，压得你喘不过气来？
turns.belief_state: 帮助来访者客观看待核心信念的功能与代价

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 确实是盔甲。有时候我甚至想把这副盔甲脱掉，哪怕只露出一小会儿真实的我，看看会发生什么。
turns.belief_state: 来访者开始萌生重构核心信念的内在动机

sessions.ending_state: 成功评估了行为实验，触及了关于完美主义与自我价值的核心信念，来访者情绪由焦虑转为深刻的反思与接纳

sessions.goal: 巩固认知重构成果，制定长期的应对策略与预防复发计划

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 晓晴，回顾我们这几次的咨询，从最初的无助和混乱，到后来敢于做行为实验，再到看到完美主义这副“盔甲”，你觉得最大的变化是什么？
turns.belief_state: 阶段性总结能够增强来访者的内在掌控感

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 我觉得我不再把脑子里冒出来的每个想法都当成绝对真理了。虽然考试成绩还是让我焦虑，但我知道这不代表我是个彻底的失败者。
turns.belief_state: 认知灵活性显著提升，能够区分事实与思维

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 这真的是一个巨大的进步。你学会了退后一步，像个科学家一样去审视自己的内心。如果接下来又遇到了低谷或者强烈的自我怀疑，你觉得你可以用什么工具来应对？
turns.belief_state: 培养来访者成为自己的治疗师

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 我可以继续写认知日记，把自动思维抓出来；另外就是记住那次和室友喝奶茶的经历，提醒自己现实往往比想象的要宽容。
turns.belief_state: 掌握了具体的CBT自我调节工具

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 听起来你已经有了一套非常实用的“急救工具箱”。不过我也想提醒你，复原的路上可能会有起伏，这很正常。如果以后旧信念又冒出来，你会怎么对自己说？
turns.belief_state: 为可能出现的症状反复做好心理准备

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 我会对自己说：“嘿，老朋友，我知道你想保护我免受伤害，但现在我不需要穿那么重的盔甲了，我可以试着松一口气。”
turns.belief_state: 对自我价值的定义变得更加包容和富有弹性

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 这句话听起来太棒了。我们的咨询也将告一段落，但你的自我探索才刚刚开始。回看这几次对话，你有什么想对自己或对我们这段合作说的吗？
turns.belief_state: 咨询关系的总结与顺利结案

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 谢谢你，老师。谢谢你没有直接给我答案，而是陪着我把那些乱麻一层一层剥开。我觉得我找回了一点点真正的自己，也准备好去迎接接下来的大学生活了。
turns.belief_state: 来访者具备了独立面对未来挑战的信心与能力

sessions.ending_state: 圆满完成阶段性咨询目标，来访者掌握了CBT核心技能，建立了更有适应性的新信念，情绪积极且稳定

sessions.goal: Introduce collaborative empirical framework and examine initial avoidance patterns around recent social invitations.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Hello Sarah. Welcome. Let us take a moment to settle in and decide what would be most useful for us to focus on during our time today.
turns.belief_state: Collaborative structure helps reduce anxiety.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Thanks for having me. Honestly, I feel a bit scattered. I spent the whole week working late on branding decks and completely avoided a birthday gathering a colleague invited me to.
turns.belief_state: If I am not working, I am wasting time or failing.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Working late provided a clear alternative to the gathering. When you noticed the invitation, what went through your mind right before you decided not to go?
turns.belief_state: Automatic thoughts bridge situations and avoidance behaviors.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I thought, they only invited me to be polite, and if I show up tired, I will just bring the whole mood down. It is better not to impose.
turns.belief_state: My friends do not actually want to spend time with me.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That sounds like a heavy conclusion to carry. Notice how that thought, they are only being polite, acts like a rule that predicts the outcome before it even happens.
turns.belief_state: Client is treating an unverified thought as absolute fact.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: It feels like a fact when I am tired. But looking at it now, I guess I do not have actual proof they did not want me there.
turns.belief_state: Maybe my assumptions are not 100 percent guaranteed.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That distinction between feeling and fact is precisely where we can test things out together. Would you be open to tracking these thoughts this week without judging yourself for having them?
turns.belief_state: Thought records build metacognitive awareness.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I can try logging them, though I am worried I will just forget or dismiss them when I am in the middle of a workday.
turns.belief_state: I might fail at doing therapy homework right.

sessions.ending_state: Collaborative thought-logging introduced, with initial hesitation noted around homework execution.

sessions.goal: Review thought log data, examine evidence regarding burdensomeness, and address a minor misunderstanding about pacing.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Welcome back, Sarah. How did you find the process of noting down those thoughts over the past week?
turns.belief_state: Reviewing logs provides concrete data for collaborative empiricism.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I filled out three entries, but to be honest, I felt like you were going to judge me for missing two days when work got overwhelming.
turns.belief_state: If I do not complete homework, my therapist will be disappointed.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: I am really glad you brought that up right away. Let us pause there. What made you anticipate judgment from me just now?
turns.belief_state: Addressing alliance ruptures immediately prevents withdrawal.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I guess I am used to school or job reviews where missing targets means failing. I felt like I did a sloppy job because I only did three.
turns.belief_state: Performance dictates my worth.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: There are no grades here, Sarah. Three entries give us plenty of material to examine. Let us look at the second entry about feeling like a burden when tired.
turns.belief_state: Reframing homework as data collection reduces performance anxiety.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Right, that was Tuesday night. I wanted to text my friend Maya, but I thought, if I tell her I am exhausted, she will think I am draining to be around.
turns.belief_state: If I show my fatigue, people will find me burdensome.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Let us examine the evidence for that. When Maya has told you about her own exhaustion in the past, how did you respond?
turns.belief_state: Perspective-taking de-biases personal assumptions.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I listened to her and brought her coffee. I did not think she was a burden at all. I actually felt glad she trusted me.
turns.belief_state: There is a double standard between how I view myself and others.

sessions.ending_state: Rupture regarding homework expectation successfully resolved; double standard in interpersonal evaluation uncovered.

sessions.goal: Design a small behavioral experiment to test the prediction about reaching out first.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Hello Sarah. Last week we noticed a clear double standard in how you judge your own fatigue versus Maya's. How has that sat with you?
turns.belief_state: Connecting past insights to current motivation.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: It made me realize I hold myself to an impossible standard. But knowing it intellectually is different from actually changing how I act.
turns.belief_state: Intellectual insight does not automatically equal emotional belief change.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That is a very astute observation. That is why CBT relies on behavioral experiments rather than just talk. Are you willing to design a small test for this week?
turns.belief_state: Behavioral experiments test core beliefs directly.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: What kind of test? If it involves calling a large group, my anxiety is going to veto it.
turns.belief_state: Experiments will be overwhelming and intolerable.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Definitely not a large group. What about sending a low-pressure text message to one person, perhaps Maya, admitting you are tired but just wanted to say hello, without asking for anything heavy?
turns.belief_state: Graduated exposure minimizes panic while challenging assumptions.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I could send a meme or just a quick check-in. But what if she leaves me on read? That would prove she is annoyed.
turns.belief_state: Reaching out first exposes me to rejection.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That is a specific prediction: being left on read means annoyance. How else might someone leave a message unread?
turns.belief_state: Generating alternative explanations for ambiguous social cues.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: They might just be busy at work, like I often am. I suppose it does not automatically mean they hate me.
turns.belief_state: Other interpretations of delayed replies are plausible.

sessions.ending_state: Behavioral experiment collaboratively designed around a low-pressure text message to test rejection prediction.

sessions.goal: 建立咨询同盟，探索项目延期事件带来的负面情绪及其背后的自动思维

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 林晓你好，很高兴能在这里陪你一起聊聊。你今天来到这里，最希望我们一起探讨或者有什么想要解决的困扰吗？
turns.belief_state: 咨询师持有倾听和合作的立场

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 老师你好。其实我最近过得很煎熬。上个月我负责的数据项目因为系统漏洞延期了两周，虽然最后解决了，但我的主管虽然没说什么，我自己却觉得天要塌下来一样，整晚睡不着。
turns.belief_state: 我犯了错误，这证明我很糟糕

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 听到项目延期让你经历这么大的痛苦，晚上也睡不好，这一定很不容易。能跟我说说，当你想起项目延期这件事时，脑子里最先冒出的想法是什么吗？
turns.belief_state: 需要通过自动化思维记录来识别核心信念

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 我脑子里一直有个声音在说：‘你太失败了连这点事都做不好，大家肯定都在背后笑话你，你根本不配在这个职位上。’
turns.belief_state: 如果我失败了，我就毫无价值

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 这是一个非常沉重的想法。我们可以把它看作是你脑海中的一个‘自动思维’。当这个想法出现时，它带给你的情绪冲击是什么样的呢？
turns.belief_state: 区分想法与事实是CBT的第一步

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 就是胸口发闷，喘不上气，觉得整个人都在往下沉。我从小到大都是这样，只要考砸一次或者表现不好，就会觉得自己一无是处。
turns.belief_state: 我的自我价值完全取决于外部表现

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 从小到大都背负着这种‘必须表现完美’的尺子，这让你走得太累了。我们今天只是初步理清了这个线索，你愿意在接下来的时间里，和我们一起像科学家一样，去检验一下这把尺子是否真的那么绝对吗？
turns.belief_state: 确立合作性经验主义的框架

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 我也很想改变这种状态，但说实话，我心里还是很不踏实，总觉得如果我不严格要求自己，就会彻底完蛋。
turns.belief_state: 完美主义是保护我免受惩罚的唯一方式

sessions.ending_state: 识别了项目延期引发的核心自动思维，建立了初步的认知行为框架，但客户仍对放弃完美主义标准存有戒备与恐惧

sessions.goal: 绘制认知模型，检查“条件化假设”并设计第一次行为实验

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 林晓，上次我们聊到你对完美的严苛要求。这周过得怎么样？有没有注意到那个‘如果我做不好，我就是失败者’的想法在什么时候出现得比较多？
turns.belief_state: 通过复盘家庭作业促进自我觉察

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 这周组里分配了新任务，我一接到任务就又开始焦虑了。我发现自己总是在脑子里写剧本，预测各种会出错的场景，然后疯狂加班去检查每一个细节。
turns.belief_state: 只有过度准备才能阻止灾难发生

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 这种‘写剧本’和‘疯狂加班’就像是一套防御机制，在帮应对你内心的恐惧。但它同时也让你消耗了大量的心力。我们能不能把它画成一个循环图：事件-自动思维-情绪-行为？
turns.belief_state: 可视化认知模型有助于客户客观审视问题

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 看着这个图，我突然发现，其实我的行为反而在不断强化那个恐惧——因为我越加班检查，就越觉得这件事极其危险，必须由我完美把控。
turns.belief_state: 我的防御行为实际上维持了我的焦虑

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 你的觉察力真的很敏锐！你精准地抓住了维持这个困境的关键。既然我们看到了这个循环，你觉得有没有可能做一点点微小的调整，来打破它？
turns.belief_state: 鼓励客户主动参与干预方案的设计

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 调整？比如什么调整？我不敢直接摆烂不检查，那样我会一整天都无法专心工作。
turns.belief_state: 任何降低标准的小动作都可能引发灾难

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 我们不需要跨越式地‘摆烂’。我们可以设计一个安全的行为实验：比如这次周报检查，和平时比减少一次复查，看看‘灾难性的后果’是否真的会发生，好吗？
turns.belief_state: 行为实验需要循序渐进，确保安全可控

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 只减少一次复查……听起来好像没那么可怕，但我心里还是有点打鼓。不过，我可以试一试。
turns.belief_state: 愿意尝试小幅度的改变，但仍有保留

sessions.ending_state: 完成了认知循环模型的绘制，客户对自身焦虑维持机制有了结构性理解，并同意进行轻量级的行为实验

sessions.goal: 复盘行为实验结果，探讨深层核心信念及其童年根源

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 林晓，欢迎回来。我特别想听听，你上周尝试的那个‘减少一次周报复查’的实验进行得怎么样？结果符合你的预期吗？
turns.belief_state: 通过复盘实验数据挑战旧信念

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 说实话，结果让我挺意外的。我少检查了一次，按时交了上去，结果主管什么也没说，甚至还顺手点了个赞。我并没有像想象中那样被开除或者被嘲笑。
turns.belief_state: 并非每一次不完美都会带来灾难性的惩罚

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 太棒了！你的实验数据给了我们一个非常有力的反证。当现实和你的预期不一致时，你的内心有什么样的感受？
turns.belief_state: 强化实验成功带来的认知修正

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 松了一口气，但紧接着又冒出一个想法：‘这次只是运气好，主管没仔细看。下次肯定没这么幸运。’你看，我好像总是不肯放过自己。
turns.belief_state: 旧的核心信念依然强大，试图将积极证据归因于运气

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 你看得很清楚，哪怕有了现实证据，那个旧的核心信念还是想把功劳归结为‘运气’。这说明这套信念在你的生命里待了很久，它一直在试图保护你。我们能顺着它往回看吗？这把‘只有优秀才安全’的尺子，是从什么时候开始拿在手里的？
turns.belief_state: 探索核心信念的童年起源

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 我想起了小时候……我每次考了第二名回家，我爸就会问我：‘第一名是谁？为什么扣了这2分？’当时我就觉得，只有拿第一名，爸爸才会真正抱我、对我笑。
turns.belief_state: 我必须通过卓越的成绩来换取爱与安全感

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 一个小女孩为了得到爸爸的爱与认可，不得不把所有的重担都扛在肩上，把‘优秀’当作通往爱的唯一门票。这真的太不容易了。当时的那个小女孩，现在还能分清‘表现’和‘自我价值’的区别吗？
turns.belief_state: 引导客户区分儿童时期的生存策略与成年后的真实自我

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: （眼眶湿润）好像……好像一直以来，我都分不清。我把当年的那个小女孩带到了现在的工作岗位上，要求她永远不能犯错。这其实挺残酷的。
turns.belief_state: 开始对内心的完美主义产生批判性反思，但仍有未解的痛楚

sessions.ending_state: 通过行为实验反证和童年根源的追溯，客户触及了核心信念的源头，体验到了初步的自我同情，但仍需在后续会谈中巩固并建立新的自我评价体系

sessions.goal: Establish collaborative framework, identify presenting problem, and begin socializing the client to the cognitive model.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Hello Elena. Thank you for coming in today. I want to make sure we use our time well, so let us set an agenda together. What feels most pressing for us to focus on during this first session?
turns.belief_state: collaborative orientation

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Hi. Well, I have been feeling completely stuck lately. At work, every time a client asks for a revision, my mind instantly jumps to the conclusion that I am terrible at my job and going to get fired. It exhausts me.
turns.belief_state: If a project is not flawless, I am an utter failure as a professional.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That sounds incredibly heavy to carry around every single day. When that thought pops up about being terrible at your job, what happens immediately afterward in your body or your mood?
turns.belief_state: linking thoughts to emotional and physiological reactions

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: My chest gets really tight, and I just feel this wave of shame. I usually avoid checking my email for hours, which honestly just makes the anxiety pile up even more.
turns.belief_state: My mistakes are permanent evidence of my inadequacy.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: So we have a cycle here: a revision request comes in, the automatic thought of failure arises, leading to physical tension and shame, which then triggers avoidance. Does that mapping feel accurate to your experience?
turns.belief_state: cognitive model framework

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Yes, exactly. But it feels like that is just how reality is. Those thoughts feel completely true in the moment, not like something I can just change.
turns.belief_state: automatic thoughts equal absolute truth

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: It makes complete sense that they feel entirely true when they hit so fast and hard. In our work together, we are not going to force positive thinking or pretend things are easy. Instead, we can treat these thoughts as hypotheses rather than absolute facts, and test them out together.
turns.belief_state: thoughts as hypotheses

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Treating them as hypotheses sounds interesting, though I am not sure how I can do that when I am panicked. But I am willing to try if it helps quiet the noise.
turns.belief_state: open to cognitive exploration

sessions.ending_state: Collaborative formulation established; client understands the cognitive model concept and agrees to track automatic thoughts during the week.

sessions.goal: Review thought records, examine evidence for core automatic negative thoughts, and identify cognitive distortions.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Welcome back, Elena. How did you find the process of tracking your thoughts over the past week? Was there any moment that stood out?
turns.belief_state: collaborative review

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I tried doing the thought record, but honestly, it felt a bit pointless by Wednesday. I had a feedback meeting where my manager wanted changes on a banner design, and my mind instantly went back to: People only tolerate me out of obligation.
turns.belief_state: People only tolerate me out of obligation rather than genuine affection.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: I appreciate you sharing that frustration, Elena. It can feel really disheartening when the exercises feel mechanical or when the thoughts feel overwhelmingly loud. Let us look at that specific belief about being tolerated out of obligation. What was the actual evidence from that meeting?
turns.belief_state: examining objective data

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Well, my manager said she liked the overall color palette, but she wanted the typography larger so it was more readable on mobile screens.
turns.belief_state: mixture of positive feedback and constructive critique

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: And how does liking the overall color palette and asking for a typography tweak connect to people only tolerating you out of obligation?
turns.belief_state: identifying jumping to conclusions

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I guess it does not logically connect if you say it like that. In my head, any critique means the whole thing is trash, which means I am incompetent, which means they must secretly regret hiring me.
turns.belief_state: recognizing catastrophic chain

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Ah, we just caught a classic cognitive distortion in action: all-or-nothing thinking and emotional reasoning. Notice how quickly a specific design preference turned into a total judgment of your worth?
turns.belief_state: naming cognitive distortions

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Yes, seeing it written down like a chain reaction makes it look pretty extreme. But even though I see it, the heavy feeling in my stomach hasn't really gone away.

sessions.ending_state: Client gained intellectual insight into catastrophic chaining and all-or-nothing thinking, but emotional resonance of beliefs remains high.

sessions.goal: Design and review a behavioral experiment to test the hypothesis of professional inadequacy and explore alternative interpretations.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Hello Elena. Last week we noticed how an ordinary design critique triggered a catastrophic chain. How have you been feeling since then?
turns.belief_state: continuity of care

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I tried the behavioral experiment we discussed—asking a colleague directly what they thought of my layout before submitting it to the creative director. But it kind of backfired.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Tell me more about how it backfired. What happened when you asked?
turns.belief_state: exploring experimental results

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: My coworker seemed busy and just gave me a quick 'Looks fine, Elena,' without really looking up. My immediate thought was: See? She doesn't care, and I am just bothering everyone with my insecurity. I felt even worse than before.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: I am really glad you brought that up, because that is a crucial data point. It sounds like running that experiment triggered your fear of being a burden. How did you interpret her quick response in that moment?
turns.belief_state: processing experimental rupture

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I interpreted it as proof that I am annoying and incapable of figuring things out on my own. Honestly, I felt like therapy was making me overanalyze everything and making me more fragile.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: I hear you, and I really appreciate you telling me directly that it felt like therapy was making things worse. That takes courage. Let us look at what else could possibly explain your coworker's quick reply other than her being annoyed by your incompetence.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I suppose she had a major deadline of her own due that afternoon. When I think about it that way, her rushing wasn't really about me at all... but my reflex is still to make everything about my own shortcomings.

sessions.goal: 建立咨询同盟并识别社交焦虑中的自动思维

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 林伟，你好。欢迎来到这里。我想先了解一下，最近这段时间是什么情况让你决定来做咨询的？
turns.belief_state: 咨询关系建立需要安全和开放的氛围

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 老师好。主要还是因为工作上的晋升快到了，加上最近部门开会交流变多，我每天都觉得非常焦虑。我总觉得大家都在盯着我的表现，只要我有一点说错话，他们就会彻底看扁我。
turns.belief_state: 如果我表现不完美，别人就会彻底否定我

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 听到你说‘只要有一点说错话，就会彻底看扁我’，这听起来压力非常大。能具体说说最近一次让你有这种感觉的场景吗？
turns.belief_state: 需要通过具体情境来识别自动思维

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 就上周周会，我汇报时结巴了一下。当时组长没说话，我脑子里马上闪过：‘完了，他觉得我是个废物，我马上要被开除了。’接下来的整个会议我都浑身冒汗，根本听不进去别人在说什么。
turns.belief_state: 每一个细微失误都会被放大并成为嘲笑的谈资

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 这是一个很典型的自动化思维过程。当结巴发生时，你的大脑自动跳到了‘我要被开除了’这个灾难性预测。我们把这个过程记录下来，看看它当时是如何影响你的情绪和身体反应的，好吗？
turns.belief_state: 通过协同制图可以帮助来访者外化焦虑

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 嗯，好。其实理智上也知道组长可能只是在思考，但我控制不住自己往最坏的方向想，感觉自己特别没用。
turns.belief_state: 我的能力本身不足以应付目前的社交要求

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 这种自我苛求非常辛苦。你刚才提到理智上觉得组长可能在思考，这说明你的观察并没有完全被焦虑吞没。我们今天先初步梳理了这个机制，你觉得有什么收获或者不舒服的地方吗？
turns.belief_state: 检查来访者的反馈有助于发现潜在的不信任或误解

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 收获是有一些，知道了这种想法叫自动化思维。不过我还是有点担心，真的能改变吗？万一我本质上就是抗压能力太差呢？
turns.belief_state: 我的问题根深蒂固可能无法改变

sessions.ending_state: 来访者初步理解了自动思维的概念，但对自身能力的怀疑和改变的效能感仍存在保留。

sessions.goal: 检验自动思维与灾难性预测，探讨行为实验

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 林伟，过去这一周过得怎么样？上次我们谈到自动思维，你在生活中有什么新的观察吗？
turns.belief_state: 回顾家庭作业能促进认知重构的持续性

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: 我试着记录了两次。有一次在茶水间遇到总监，我打招呼时声音有点小，对方没应声。我当时差点又觉得他讨厌我，但这次我停了一下，告诉自己‘他可能只是在想事情’，没那么焦虑了。
turns.belief_state: 我可以尝试对自动化思维踩刹车

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: 这太棒了！你能主动按下暂停键，这需要很大的觉察力。后来呢？总监后来有表现出讨厌你的迹象吗？
